name: Bruxism night guard

lead: A bruxism night guard, or occlusal splint, is a hard or soft plastic appliance worn over the teeth during sleep to protect them from grinding and clenching. Custom guards are made by a dentist, while stock and boil-and-bite versions are sold over the counter.
It is used to prevent enamel wear, chipping and flattening of teeth, which over years can change how the smile looks.

paras: The guard places a plastic barrier between the upper and lower teeth so grinding forces wear the appliance instead of the enamel. It does not stop the underlying muscle activity, which is linked to stress, sleep arousals and other factors.

Splints are widely used and generally safe, but reviews find little direct evidence that they reduce tooth wear, and insufficient evidence that they cure bruxism itself; some designs may increase clenching or cause bite changes with full-time use. Ill-fitting or hard stock guards can be uncomfortable. Dental guidance is that a dentist assess for sleep apnea and other drivers.

lead: A bruxism night guard, also called an occlusal splint, bite guard or nightguard, is a removable hard or soft plastic appliance worn over the teeth, usually at night, intended to protect them from the effects of grinding and clenching. Dentists make custom versions from impressions or scans, while stock and boil-and-bite versions are sold over the counter. [1][2]

Bruxism is defined in Grokipedia, citing a 2024 international consensus, as repetitive jaw-muscle activity involving clenching, grinding, or bracing of the mandible during sleep or wakefulness, and the consensus is described as treating it as a behaviour on a continuum rather than a disorder unless it causes harm such as dental damage or pain. [1] Occlusal splints and mouthguards are described there as a first-line measure to protect teeth. [1] For appearance, the interest in night guards is that long-term grinding can flatten, chip or wear teeth and change the look of the smile. [1]

Researchers have examined whether splints reduce bruxism itself, protect against wear or help temporomandibular symptoms. Systematic reviews of occlusal splints for bruxism and for temporomandibular disorder have been published, with authors generally noting that the quality and amount of evidence is limited and that the appliance is a protective device that does not remove the underlying muscle activity. [3][4][5][2] Wear of splint materials has been the subject of its own systematic review. [6]
infobox: Removable occlusal appliance (splint) worn over teeth

Protect teeth from grinding and clenching wear [1]

paras: A night guard places a layer of plastic between the upper and lower teeth so that the forces of grinding and clenching fall on the appliance. Reviews distinguish several types of occlusal splints used for bruxism and temporomandibular disorders, including stabilisation splints and soft appliances, and compare their use. [5][2][4] Custom guards are fabricated by dentists or laboratories, while over-the-counter products are generic or heat-moulded by the wearer.

A systematic review of the wear behaviour of occlusal splint materials made by different manufacturing methods covered in vitro and in vivo testing of splints and the teeth opposing them, using materials such as polymethyl methacrylate. [6] The term night guard is also used for the trays worn for overnight tooth bleaching, which is a separate use of similar appliances. [7][8]

According to Grokipedia, sleep bruxism is thought to affect about 8 to 10 percent of adults and awake bruxism a larger share, with estimates varying by assessment method; it is considered multifactorial, with stress, sleep-related factors such as obstructive sleep apnea, medications and lifestyle all discussed as contributors. Symptoms listed include jaw muscle soreness, morning headaches, tooth sensitivity and audible grinding, and in severe cases flattened or chipped teeth, gum recession and temporomandibular joint problems. [1] That source also lists botulinum toxin injections into the masseter, behavioural therapy and treatment of underlying sleep disorders as other management approaches. [1] Because Grokipedia is AI-generated, these figures are given as a general orientation rather than as established statistics.

Bruxism is also discussed in implant dentistry, where it has traditionally been regarded as a risk factor, although a review found no consistent proof that bruxism causes implant overload and recommended a careful approach, and a polysomnography study examined sleep bruxism in patients with implants. [9][10]

A 2021 systematic review in the Journal of Dentistry examined the efficacy of occlusal splints in the treatment of bruxism, a 2020 systematic review examined oral splints for temporomandibular disorder or bruxism, and a 2023 systematic review compared types of occlusal splint for sleep bruxism. [3][4][5] A 2023 review described splint types and their effectiveness in temporomandibular disorder management. [2] Reviews in this area commonly note small trials, short follow-up and variable outcome measures, which limits conclusions about whether splints reduce tooth wear or bruxism activity itself.

Other trials have used night guards for related purposes: a controlled clinical trial applied a night guard to sleep-related dry mouth, and a randomized trial compared a betaine mouthwash with an intraoral device for dry mouth. [11][12] A 1992 double-blind controlled study and later trials used night guards to deliver 10 percent carbamide peroxide whitening gel. [7][8]

Splints are widely prescribed and reported as generally well tolerated, but reviews describe limited evidence for tooth-wear prevention and for curing bruxism. [3][4][5] Poorly fitting or hard stock guards may be uncomfortable, and splints cannot address the muscle activity or its causes such as sleep apnea or stress, for which clinical assessment is used. [1] The wear of the appliance itself, and its effect on opposing teeth, has been studied in materials research. [6]

The site's rating describes night guards as protecting teeth from being flattened by grinding over the years. The research material for this entry contained no substantive forum discussion specific to night guards, though forum users have discussed jaw clenching and cosmetic dental care in general.
